subject: snail
pitch: A garden snail on an adventure. A glossy spiral shell striped in caramel, chocolate and cream, a soft grey-green body with a pebbly texture and a slimy shine, two long eye stalks with little black eyes and two short feelers below. A tiny ladybird hitches a ride on top of the shell.
reasoning:
I'm planning the TypeScript module using the SDK, thinking through scale — real garden snails are tiny, maybe 5cm, but for this stylized adventurer design I want a slightly larger, more expressive size around a quarter meter.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton layout: a root hip joint near ground level, a spine chain running along the body from tail to head using catmull-spline points, with the shell sitting toward the back and eye stalks branching off near the front.

For the body geometry, I'm defining a tube swept along the spine using elliptical cross-sections (wider sideways, shorter vertically) so the snail's underside sits flat against the ground, with radius tapering smaller toward the tail. For the shell, I'm planning a spiral coil swept along a helical path with growing radius to mimic a snail shell.

I'll texture the shell by painting bands along the tube's length parameter, cycling between chocolate, caramel, and cream colors to create concentric stripe rings along the coil.

For positioning, I'm placing the shell on the snail's back with its axis tilted so the spiral lies roughly flat when viewed from above, sizing it so the coil's base nestles into the body. I want the coil to taper from a wide radius down to a point over about 2.5 turns, and since real snail shells are conical rather than flat, I need to add pitch along the axis so it rises like a spring while shrinking, giving that classic cone-helix shape.

Since a basic lathe can't produce a true spiral, I'm settling on a hybrid approach: a lathe-based dome for the shell's main body, painted with caramel stripe bands, combined with a tapering spiral tube wrapped around it to suggest the whorl ridges, keeping the overall construction simple enough to stay robust.

I'm deciding the coil's axis should point sideways along X so the spiral face is visible from the camera's side view, since the snail faces +Z. The spiral sweeps along that axis with increasing turns, giving the shell its conical, layered look centered near the body.

I'm shaping the whorl geometrically so each loop shrinks relative to the last, tapering both the coil radius and tube thickness from outer to inner turns to mimic a real spiral shell. I'm also adding a scaled sphere inside the coil to fill the body whorl and give the shell solidity, colored a caramel tone.

For texture, I'm planning banded coloring along the coil using paint utilities, cycling caramel, chocolate, and cream stripes based on position along the spiral, and giving the body a pebbly grey-green texture by blending colors with noise and cell-based borders to mimic a mottled, pebbled surface.

For the body shape itself, I'm sketching a snail foot as a swept path along a catmull spline, with the radius tapering narrower at the tail and wider toward the head to give it a believable organic bulge, though I'm keeping it simplified and stylized rather than fully anatomical.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up a root hip joint and then building a spine chain along the body path with named segments for tail, back, mid, neck, and head, working through how the chain's point count and span count need to line up so the joints distribute correctly along the curve.

For the shell, I'm attaching it to the back joint from the spine chain rather than the hips directly, so it rides along the body's midsection as the creature moves.

For the eye stalks, I'm building bezier sweeps that rise from the head joint using local coordinate words like left/right and up/forward instead of raw axes, with mirrored positions for each side, then placing eye spheres at the tips of the stalks.

I'm adding tiny black eyes with a small white highlight sphere for detail, plus shorter feeler sweeps below the eyes that taper from the head forward, using body-matching color for cohesion.

I'm also figuring out where the head joint actually sits along the chain since joints mark span starts rather than the path's end, so I'm approximating the head's forward offset and considering a small extra sphere bulb to bulk out the head shape.

Now I'm working out where to perch a ladybird on top of the shell—placing its dome body near the shell's top point, then defining a spiral path in the YZ plane starting from that top position with decreasing radius and a couple of turns to suggest the shell's curve beneath it.

Reworking the shell proportions, I settle on a smaller tube radius and outer radius so the shell sinks slightly into the body, placing its center around [0, 0.16, -0.02]. The spiral coil lies flat with pitch 0 in the YZ plane, tapering its tube radius from outer to inner whorls, and I consider adding a dome-shaped fill scaled along X to match the planar coil shape.

I'm positioning a ladybird ornament on the shell's outer top whorl, using a squashed sphere for the body with a small dark head sphere and tiny black spotted dots stuck onto its surface via angle-based placement, all rigged to the body's back bone.

For the main body sweep, I work out a radius function that varies width (rx) along the tail-to-head taper while keeping height (ry) mostly constant so the belly stays grounded at y=0, using a shift function to compensate when ry changes. I plan pebbly body texture through a noise/cell-based paint function mixing body-green tones, and a striped spiral paint for the shell alternating caramel, chocolate, and cream bands based on path position.

I'm figuring out eye stalks and feelers as bezier sweeps extending from head-local offsets, mirrored left/right with a sign variable, tipped with small dark eye spheres and tiny white highlights.

Finally I'm checking the spiral's radius decay across 2.2 turns to make sure neighboring whorls don't overlap too much, adjusting tube thickness and turn ratio so the coil reads as a tidy conical shell rather than a jumble of overlapping rings.

Writing paint functions...
